beats.text: Counting becomes easier when we organize choices. Three shirt choices and two trouser choices create six outfits because every shirt can pair with every trouser. The grid represents the independent stages of the choice, not probabilities by itself.

Now choose a first and second person from four distinct people, without repetition. There are four possibilities first and three afterward. The twelve ordered selections distinguish who was chosen first, so swapping the same two people creates another outcome.

If we only want a two-person committee, order no longer matters. Each unordered pair was counted twice, once in each order, so divide by two. The six edges connecting four labeled people represent the six distinct committees.

Allowing repetition changes the count again. A two-position code with four symbols has four choices at each position, making sixteen possibilities. Before choosing a formula, decide whether order matters and whether a chosen object can be used again.

practice.prompt: How many ordered arrangements of three different books can be chosen from five different books? Explain each factor.
practice.answer: There are 5 choices first, 4 second, and 3 third, so 5·4·3=60.

practice.prompt: How many three-book groups can be chosen from those five books if order does not matter? Explain the division.
practice.answer: Each group has 3!=6 orderings, so the count is 60/6=10.

practice.prompt: How many four-digit codes use digits 0–9 if repetition and leading zero are allowed? How would excluding repeated digits change the result?
practice.answer: With repetition there are 10⁴=10,000 codes. Without repetition, there are 10·9·8·7=5,040.

takeaway: Identify stages, order, and repetition before counting; divide only when you know exactly how many times each outcome was counted.
scope: The product rule, ordered choices, combinations, and repeated symbols.
title: Combinatorics
objective: Count using sums, products, permutations, combinations, and inclusion-exclusion.
